The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore, introduced in 1993 as a more robust and contemporary evolution of the original Royal Oak, quickly established itself as a cornerstone of the brandÃ¢ÂÂs modern identity. Reference 25770ST, produced in the early 2000s, belongs to a generation of Offshore models that explored bolder color variations and enhanced wrist presence.
The present example, distinguished by its vibrant red Ã¢ÂÂpetite TapisserieÃ¢ÂÂ dial, is emblematic of this creative period, during which Audemars Piguet experimented with more expressive aesthetics while retaining the collectionÃ¢ÂÂs signature design codes. The combination of a stainless steel case, chronograph functionality, and striking dial configuration reflects the modelÃ¢ÂÂs dual appeal as both a technical instrument and a statement piece.
Offshore references from this era have increasingly attracted collector interest, particularly those featuring uncommon dial colors. As such, the present watch offers an opportunity to acquire a well-preserved example of a distinctive and increasingly sought-after variation within the Royal Oak Offshore lineage.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore Ã¢ÂÂYellowÃ¢ÂÂ, reference 25770ST.OO.D009XX.02, is a striking example of the collectionÃ¢ÂÂs early 2000s bold color explorations. Its vivid yellow Ã¢ÂÂpetite TapisserieÃ¢ÂÂ dial immediately commands attention, exemplifying Audemars PiguetÃ¢ÂÂs adventurous approach to design while maintaining the signature robustness of the Offshore line.Housed in a stainless-steel case with chronograph functionality and a date display, the watch combines technical sophistication with a sporty, contemporary aesthetic. The octagonal bezel with exposed screws reinforces the modelÃ¢ÂÂs distinctive architectural presence.Preserved in very good overall condition, this exceptional example offers collectors a rare opportunity to acquire a vibrant and highly desirable iteration of the Royal Oak Offshore.

The ÃÂlÃÂ©gante fromÂ F.P. Journe was introduced in 2014 andÂ represents one of the most unconventional, unexpected and yet forward-thinking creations from FranÃÂ§ois-Paul Journe.
Departing from traditional mechanics, the ÃÂlÃÂ©gante is powered by the in-house caliber 1210, an electro-mechanical quartz movement engineered to the standards of haute horlogerie. Its defining innovation is a motion-detection system: after approximately 30 minutes of inactivity, the hands stop to conserve energy, automatically resetting to the correct time when the watch is worn again. This playful, engaging and innovation idea allows for an exceptional battery life of up to 18 years.
The present example is housed in a lightweight grade 5 titanium tonneau case measuring 48mm, giving the watch a masculine presence with excellent ergonomics. The matte finished case contrasts nicely with the white lacquered dial, featuring unmistakable and signature F.P. Journe Arabic numerals, blued steel hands, subsidiary seconds at 6, and motion detector in an open window at 4:30.Â 
The ÃÂlÃÂ©gante occupies a unique position within the work of F.P. Journe, a bold embrace of innovation that prioritizes practicality without sacrificing craftsmanship. Originally conceived in 40mm and with female collectors in mind, the 48mm titanium variant has since gained a broader following, appreciated for its ingenuity and everyday usability.

Crafted in a distinctive tortoise-inspired form, the TortueÃ¢ÂÂconceived in 1912 by Louis CartierÃ¢ÂÂstands among the earliest shaped wristwatches by Cartier, predating even the Tank. In 1928, the model evolved into the Tortue Monopoussoir, CartierÃ¢ÂÂs first chronograph, featuring start, stop, and reset functions operated via a single pusher integrated into the crown.
The present example is part of the Collection PrivÃÂ©e Cartier Paris, produced between 1998 and 2008 as a revival of the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs mechanical watchmaking heritage. It is powered by the calibre 045MC, developed by Techniques HorlogÃÂ¨res AppliquÃÂ©es (THA) EbaucheÃ¢ÂÂa joint venture between Vianney Halter, Denis Flageollet, and FranÃÂ§ois-Paul Journe.
Presented in white gold, the watch features an Art Deco-inspired dial with blue triangular accents, an outer minute track with inverted Ã¢ÂÂTÃ¢ÂÂ markers, the Cartier signature, and an oversized Roman numeral at 12 oÃ¢ÂÂclock. A refined and historically significant timepiece, this example offers collectors the opportunity to acquire one of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs most technically and aesthetically compelling creations.

Introduced in 2016 and discontinued in 2023, the reference 116500LN marks a significant chapter in the evolution of the Rolex Daytona. It is the first stainless steel iteration to feature a black Cerachrom ceramic bezel, offering enhanced scratch resistance while subtly recalling the aesthetic of early four-digit Daytonas with their black acrylic inserts.
Crafted in stainless steel and measuring 40 mm, the watch retains the modelÃ¢ÂÂs iconic proportions and balanced wrist presence. It is powered by the self-winding chronograph calibre 4130, entirely developed and manufactured in-house by Rolex.
Offered as a complete set, this reference stands as a defining modern classicÃ¢ÂÂan essential acquisition for both seasoned collectors and those seeking to establish a discerning collection.

The Rolex Daytona reference 116509 stands among the most characterful interpretations of the model, combining the sporting pedigree of the Daytona with the understated luxury of white gold. While the Daytona has existed in stainless steel and yellow gold since the 1960s, it was not until the late 1990s that Rolex introduced a white gold variant, with the addition of a matching full white gold bracelet arriving in the mid-2000s.
Launched in 2004, the present reference exemplifies this evolution, pairing its precious metal construction with a refined black dial accented by subtle red details. The result is a highly versatile and stylish timepiece, equally suited for daily wear or more formal occasions.
Offered as a full set and preserved in a very appealing condition, this example represents an appealing opportunity to acquire a distinctive and sophisticated modern Daytona.

Ã¢ÂÂInvenit et FecitÃ¢ÂÂ (Ã¢ÂÂinvented and madeÃ¢ÂÂ) is the guiding philosophy of FranÃÂ§ois-Paul Journe and defines every creation of F.P. Journe.
The ChronomÃÂ¨tre Bleu is distinguished by its purity, presenting a time-only display that underscores JourneÃ¢ÂÂs dedication to chronometric precision and restrained design. Crafted in tantalum, a rare and highly durable metal with a distinctive grey-blue tone, the 39 mm case is paired with a captivating blue dial, lending the watch a subtle yet unmistakable presence.
Appreciated by collectors for its understated execution and faithful expression of the brandÃ¢ÂÂs watchmaking philosophy, the present example, presented on behalf of its original owner, is offered with its full complement of original accessories.

Launched in 2019, the reference 5212 by Patek Philippe is distinguished by its vintage-inspired aesthetic and highly original dial design. Rendered in a silvery opaline tone, the dial features unique typography based on the handwriting of one of the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs designers, lending the watch a distinctive and personal character. It also marks the brandÃ¢ÂÂs first wristwatch to incorporate a weekly calendar complication.
Housed in a 40 mm stainless steel case, the watch combines modern proportions with refined details, including a stepped bezel and elegantly shaped lugs, resulting in a sophisticated and well-balanced profile. Offered with its original accessories, this example presents an appealing opportunity for collectors seeking a contemporary yet characterful Patek Philippe timepiece.

Launched in 2017, the Calatrava reference 6006G by Patek Philippe continues a distinctive lineage that began with the reference 5000 in 1992 and evolved through the 6000G. Both models are defined by their unconventional display, combining an off-centred subsidiary seconds with a peripheral date indicated along the outer edge of the dial.
The 6006G reinterprets this concept with a more contemporary aesthetic, featuring a graphic two-tone dial and clean Arabic numerals that lend the watch a subtly sportier character while retaining the elegance of the Calatrava line.
Housed in a 39 mm white gold case, the present example is offered in very good condition, recently serviced, and accompanied by its presentation box, Certificate of Origin, and full set of accessories.

Renowned for its uncompromising craftsmanship, Patek Philippe has long been synonymous with the art of the Heure Universelle, a complication perfected in collaboration with master watchmaker Louis Cottier. His ingenious systemÃ¢ÂÂdisplaying 24 time zones simultaneouslyÃ¢ÂÂremains the foundation of the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs celebrated world time watches, widely regarded as the ultimate companions for the most sophisticated traveler.
Introduced in 2006, the reference 5130P-001 embodies this legacy in its most refined form. Housed in a slim platinum case of Calatrava-like elegance, it features a striking dial with a grey guillochÃÂ© center, encircled by a ring of 24 cities corresponding to global time zones. The sapphire case back reveals the calibre 240 HU with micro-rotor, enabling its notably slender profile.
A harmonious blend of technical ingenuity and understated elegance, the present example stands as a superb expression of Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs mastery in world time watchmaking.

Inspired by Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs aviatorÃ¢ÂÂs watches of 1936, the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time collection seamlessly blends heritage and modernity, establishing itself as a distinctive pillar within the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs contemporary offerings.
The reference 7234G, housed in a 37.5 mm white gold case, features a practical dual time zone mechanism displaying local and home time via luminous hands, complemented by applied Arabic numerals for optimal legibility. True to the spirit of the Pilot line, it achieves a harmonious balance between functionality and clarity, resulting in a timepiece of strong character and enduring appeal.

Unveiled at the 1998 Basel Fair, the reference 5070 by Patek Philippe marked a bold and unexpected departure for the manufacture. At a time when the brand had long focused on highly complicated chronographs, the 5070 reintroduced a simple chronographÃ¢ÂÂyet did so in striking fashion, with an oversized 42 mm yellow gold case, the largest ever produced in series by the maison at the time.
Despite its modern proportions, the design was deeply rooted in history, drawing direct inspiration from the vintage reference 2512, notably through its stepped bezel and bi-compax dial layout. Beneath the caseback beats the revered Lemania-based calibre 2310Ã¢ÂÂalso forming the base of the early A. Lange & SÃÂ¶hne DatographÃ¢ÂÂmaking the 5070 the final chapter in Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs use of this legendary movement, just before the shift toward fully in-house chronograph calibres.
The present example belongs to the first series of production, echoing the iconic yellow gold and black dial configuration of its historic predecessor. Both a bold statement piece and a significant transitional reference, it represents the closing of one era and the dawn of another in Patek Philippe chronograph history.

Under the direction of Jean-Jacques Cartier, the London branch of Cartier became the most unconventional of the three maisons, embracing bold forms and larger case designs that reflected the creative spirit of 1960s London. At its core, Cartier has always been driven by design, and few models express this more clearly than the Baignoire.
Named for its distinctive bathtub-shaped case, the Baignoire has become an enduring icon within the Cartier repertoire. The present London example, bearing the coveted Ã¢ÂÂJCÃ¢ÂÂ stamp and 1965 English hallmarks for 18k gold, is particularly noteworthy. Research suggests that Baignoire models fitted with gold bracelets were produced in extremely limited numbersÃ¢ÂÂonly three are believed to have been sold through the London boutique. One was acquired by acclaimed actor Laurence Harvey, another one by American director Josef Losey and a third one by another a gentleman from the film industry.
Having previously handled the other two known examples, SothebyÃ¢ÂÂs is pleased to offer the present lot, which retains very attractive proportions. This watch stands as a significant piece from Cartier LondonÃ¢ÂÂs most creative era.

The Cartier Ceinture is one of the most distinctive yet understated designs within the rich history of Cartier. Originally introduced in 1927 and relaunched in 1973Ã¢ÂÂ74 in 25 mm and 27 mm formats, it reflects a period defined by bold experimentation in case design, showcasing CartierÃ¢ÂÂs ability to reinterpret classical elegance through a modern, architectural lens.
Its name, derived from the French word for Ã¢ÂÂbelt,Ã¢ÂÂ refers to the defining feature of the watch: a square case framed by extended brancards resembling a belt buckle. This strong geometric identity sets the Ceinture apart from more widely recognised Cartier shapes, while remaining faithful to the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs enduring principles of proportion, balance, and refinement.
Typically fitted with classical dials featuring Roman numerals and chemin de fer minute tracks, the model achieves a compelling contrast between the assertiveness of its case and the restraint of its dial design. This duality, bold in form yet classical in execution, is emblematic of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs design language of the period.
Produced in relatively limited numbers, the Ceinture has long remained a connoisseurÃ¢ÂÂs choice. Increasingly appreciated today, it stands out for its unique silhouette and its place within the broader narrative of 1970s design.

The Bamboo Coussin is a distinctive Cartier creation that perfectly reflects the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs enduring fascination with form, culture and artistic expression. Introduced in the early 1970s and produced in both menÃ¢ÂÂs and ladiesÃ¢ÂÂ sizes, the Bamboo model stands as a bold yet elegant interpretation of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs design language during a highly creative period in its history.
Its design draws clear inspiration from Asian aesthetics, a source of influence that Cartier had been exploring since the early 20th century. This cultural dialogue first emerged with iconic creations such as the Tank Chinoise in 1922, followed by a series of exquisite Art Deco clocks and objets dÃ¢ÂÂart that incorporated geometric structure and non-European motifs. The Bamboo Coussin continues this tradition, translating the organic rhythm of bamboo into sculptural gold elements that frame the case with both strength and fluidity.The present example, a large-size model in yellow gold, is particularly rare and desirable. Its harmonious proportions and textured gold construction give it a strong visual presence on the wrist, while retaining the refined elegance expected of Cartier. 
The present lot not only serves as a functional watch but also as a wearable piece of design history: an enduring testament to CartierÃ¢ÂÂs ability to merge cultural inspiration with timeless craftsmanship.

The design of the Cartier Santos has evolved subtly over time, giving rise to several distinct early variations. Among them, the Santos Droit stands as one of the earliest and rarest, of which the present watchÃ¢ÂÂdating to 1911Ã¢ÂÂis an exceptional example. Unlike the more familiar Santos-Dumont, it features elongated, flowing lugs and a square, chamfered bezel secured from beneath, highlighting a more architectural and experimental design language.
The dial features the signature Ã¢ÂÂCartier Paris Bte S.G.D.G.Ã¢ÂÂ (BrevetÃÂ© Sans Garantie du Gouvernement), a marking used in France to denote a patented invention without state guarantee. Frequently found on early 20th-century Cartier timepieces, this inscription reflects the innovative and exploratory nature of these watches during a formative period in wristwatch design. While not necessarily indicating a prototype in the strictest sense, it strongly suggests an early production piece, created at a time when designs were still being refined and patents actively registered.
The origins of the Santos date to 1904, when Louis Cartier created one of the first wristwatches for aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont. By 1911, the model had entered commercial production, making the present example a remarkable witness to the very beginnings of serially produced wristwatchesÃ¢ÂÂan object that remains as forward-looking today as it was over a century ago.

The Obus takes its name from the French word for Ã¢ÂÂshellÃ¢ÂÂ and was, according to legend, inspired by the shape of artillery shells. 
Introduced in 1923 by Cartier, the model features distinctive rounded, bullet shaped lugs that elegantly integrate the strap with the watch case. It stands among the earliest and most recognizable expressions of Ã¢ÂÂfancyÃ¢ÂÂ lug design in wristwatch history. The Obus has remained a popular model over the decades. Its periodic re-releases reflect subtle adaptations to contemporary tastes while preserving its core design elements.
The present example, dating to 1925, displays pleasing proportions and a strong graphics. A compelling reflection of the interwar period, it captures a moment when the influences of modernity and conflict subtly permeated design, giving rise to forms that remain strikingly relevant today.

The Pilote Baguette ÃÂ  cadres inclinÃÂ©, also known as a driverÃ¢ÂÂs watch, represents one of the most unusual and inventive designs by Cartier. First introduced around 1936, during a period of remarkable innovation in watchmaking, it reflects a time when the wristwatch emerged as the primary focus of creativity despite the economic challenges following the Wall Street Crash. By the mid-1930s, wristwatch production had surpassed that of pocket watches, alongside the emergence of icons such as the Rolex Oyster Perpetual, Patek Philippe Calatrava, and Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso.
Conceived for motorists, the model features a distinctive triangular prism-shaped case with an inclined dial, allowing the time to be read while keeping both hands on the wheelÃ¢ÂÂan elegant fusion of practicality and design. Crafted in 18ct yellow gold and dating to circa 1945Ã¢ÂÂ46, the present example is further distinguished by its rare rear-wound configuration, preserving the purity of its geometric form, and is accompanied by its gold deployant buckle.
Produced only in very small numbers, with limited examples made in the 1930s and even fewer in the following decades, these driverÃ¢ÂÂs watches remain exceptionally rare. The present watch stands as a striking testament to the ingenuity and experimental spirit that defined one of the most creative eras in 20th-century horology.

Audemars Piguet has long been revered for its unparalleled artistry in skeletonisation, creating timepieces that transcend functionality to become works of art.The present Reference 35693BA, dating from the early 1980's, is a superb reflection of this tradition.This unique piece, as confirmed by the Certificat d'AuthenticitÃÂ© et d'ExclusivitÃÂ© accompanying the watch, is encased in glowing yellow gold. It harmonises technical brilliance with extraordinary aesthetic allure.Â What elevates this piece to a true rarity is the possibility that it was a special commission. Audemars Piguet has long been known for creating bespoke pieces for discerning clients, and the unique combination of the oversized case, housing the ultra thin skeletonized movement, designed as a pocket watch but made with lugs to be worn as a wristwatch strongly suggests that this was no ordinary production watch.Â The skeletonised movement is based on the Calibre 5020. This manual movement is highly praised by collectors for its ultra thin and intricate architecture. It is the perfect canvas for skilled watchmakers to create a superb fully hand decorated masterpiece. On this lot, each component has been exquisitely hollowed out, revealing the mechanical heart of the watch in a stunning display of craftsmanship. The gear trains, escapement, and barrel spring are all laid bare, allowing the wearer to witness the intricate interplay of parts that bring the timepiece to life. Audemars Piguet, always at the forefront of this delicate craft, created an atelier dedicated exclusively to openworking, further solidifying its reputation as a leader in this horological art.Â Recently discovered in a private collection and fresh to the market, this timepiece is an important discovery that does not only exemplifies the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs commitment to pushing the boundaries of design and engineering, but also likely represents a highly exclusive creation, tailored for a collector who sought something truly unique. Its rarity, combined with the extraordinary craftsmanship and audacious design, makes it a treasure for the connoisseur, an emblem of both technical prowess and luxurious artistry.

Launched in the early 2000s, the Portugieser Tourbillon MystÃÂ¨re Squelette was a limited-edition version of IWCÃ¢ÂÂs positively iconic nautical-inspired model, the Portugieser, in platinum, pink, white, and yellow gold, with 50 made in each metal. The present model, in its impressive 44mm platinum case, is number 8 out of 50 made in this material.Â 
Its movement, cal. 50910 is skeletonisedÂ and boasts a floating one-minute tourbillon at 12 oÃ¢ÂÂclock, with small seconds and a seven-day power-reserve display at 9 oÃ¢ÂÂclock. The movement is hand-engraved and finished throughout, a techique usually reserved by IWC for select editions and commemorations. The engraving of the gold rotor can additionally be appreciated through the sapphire caseback. Highly rich in detail, the technical ingenuity of the engraving makes it a highly original movement for IWC and brings additional appeal to this in-house IWC tourbillon movement.
The exclusivity, technical ingenuity and impressive craftsmanship of the present model, offered in great condition, presents an opportunity to acquire an attractive and collectable contemporary timepiece from the instantly recognisable Portugieser family.

The aesthetics of the reference 43040 is truly an incomparable masterpiece by Vacheron Constantin. Featuring a jump hour complication, the watch displays time through a jumping hour aperture with a minute indicator that revolves around the dial. The present model draws inspiration from previous Art Deco models, infusing it with a retro and sentimental style that is accentuated by its stepped bezel and straight lugs.Â The arrangement of the dial in this Jump Hour timepiece is visually mesmerizing. At the center, a delicate hand-applied guillochÃÂ© pattern adds a touch of elegance. The hour markers and the frame surrounding the hour window are crafted from yellow gold, enhancing the watchÃ¢ÂÂs overall aesthetic with a sense of opulence and refinement.This particular lot is a collector's dream. It is preserved in spectacular condition and is accompanied by its most complete set of accessories, making it the perfect example of this highly sought-after model.

A rare and elegant Ã¢ÂÂClassique TourbillonÃ¢ÂÂ reference 3657 by Breguet exemplifies the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs mastery of classical watchmaking and high complication. Featuring coin edge fluting and welded lugs, the watch combines technical sophistication with timeless refinement.
Produced in extremely limited numbers, the reference 3657 reflects BreguetÃ¢ÂÂs enduring commitment to the legacy of Abraham-Louis Breguet. It is powered by the manually wound calibre 560.1, an evolution of the earlier calibre 560, finished to the highest standards and visible through the case back. At its heart lies the tourbillon, a complication invented by Breguet in 1795.
The dial showcases an innovative retrograde 24-hour indication and power reserve. The silvered, engine-turned guillochÃÂ© dial, with blued Breguet hands and Roman numerals reflects the houseÃ¢ÂÂs dedication to artisanal finishing and visual harmony. The dial is overall thoughtfully laid out, maintaining legibility without sacrificing the intricate information displayed. 
Rarely seen on the market, the reference 3657 represents a compelling opportunity for collectors seeking a refined and technically accomplished timepiece.

Embodying a legacy of innovation and mechanical excellence, the Edward Piguet collection pays tribute to one of the founding figures of Audemars Piguet. Inspired by Art Deco design, it is defined by its elegant curved rectangular case and its use of refined complications.
Unveiled at the Salon International de la Haute Horlogerie in 2001, the present model is distinguished by its tourbillon and an exceptionally rare rutilated quartz dial. Formed by nature, each dial is unique, its delicate structure requiring a meticulous process of slow and meticulous sanding and polishing rather than conventional machining.
The interplay between this striking mineral dial and the traditional tourbillon creates a timepiece of both technical sophistication and strong visual identity. It is bold and elegant at the same time.
Rutilated quartz is also often associated with metaphysical qualities and has long been used in practices such as feng shui or as a symbolic talisman.
Preserved in excellent condition, the present example offers a rare opportunity to acquire a distinctive and highly collectible expression of Audemars PiguetÃ¢ÂÂs craftsmanship.

Within the repertoire of Girard-Perregaux, the Tourbillon Sous Trois Ponts dÃ¢ÂÂOr remains one of the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs most emblematic creations. Its origins trace back to a patent filed by Constant Girard in 1884, with an early example earning a gold medal at the Paris Universal Exhibition in 1889.
Reimagined as a wristwatch in 1991 for the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs 200th anniversary, following years of development, the model required the miniaturisation of its architecture while preserving its defining feature: the three gold bridges displayed on the dial side. Far from purely decorative, these bridges are integral to the movement, supporting the mainspring barrel, the gear train and hands, and the tourbillon cage respectively.
The result is a composition of remarkable clarity and symmetry, concealing a highly complex construction beneath its refined appearance. Offered complete with its full set of accessories, the present example represents a compelling opportunity to acquire one of horologyÃ¢ÂÂs most iconic and technically significant tourbillon wristwatches.

The Audemars Piguet Ã¢ÂÂJohn SchaefferÃ¢ÂÂ Reference 25798OR in pink gold is part of one of the most intriguing and underappreciated series of complicated wristwatches produced by Audemars Piguet during the 1990s. Created as a tribute to a unique historical commission, this model belongs to a small and highly exclusive group of minute repeating wristwatches developed in the mid-1990s, at a time when the manufacture was reasserting its mastery of traditional complications following the quartz crisis.Â The origin of the Ã¢ÂÂJohn SchaefferÃ¢ÂÂ name dates back to the early 20th century, when Audemars Piguet produced a highly unusual minute repeating wristwatch for the American industrialist John Wallace Schaeffer. Interestingly, historical records and later reinterpretations reveal variations in the spelling of the nameÃ¢ÂÂsometimes rendered as Ã¢ÂÂSchaefferÃ¢ÂÂ and at other times Ã¢ÂÂShaefferÃ¢ÂÂÃ¢ÂÂa discrepancy that has persisted over time and is reflected in different examples and references associated with the series. This subtle inconsistency has become part of the history surrounding these watches, further emphasising their unique and somewhat enigmatic character.The original commission was distinguished by its unconventional display, using the letters of the ownerÃ¢ÂÂs name in place of traditional hour markers, and left a lasting impression within the brandÃ¢ÂÂs heritage. Decades later, Audemars Piguet revisited this remarkable piece by creating a dedicated line of minute repeaters inspired by it, combining historical narrative with contemporary technical innovation.Â The Reference 25798OR stands out within this series for its distinctive display, featuring jumping hours and a non-traditional indication, offering a modern reinterpretation of timekeeping while preserving the poetic complexity of a chiming mechanism. Produced in extremely limited numbers as part of a broader but still highly restricted production of Ã¢ÂÂJohn SchaefferÃ¢ÂÂ repeaters, these watches remain exceptionally rare on the market. Today, the Reference 25798OR is appreciated not only for its rarity, but also for its unique blend of historical inspiration, technical sophistication, and unconventional design. It represents a compelling opportunity for collectors to acquire a piece that encapsulates both the legacy of early 20th-century innovation and the creative resurgence of complicated watchmaking in the 1990s.

description_block:
Produced between 1998 and 2003, the Girard-Perregaux Opera series comprised a trilogy of highly complicated wristwatches built around the minute-repeating complication. Among the most ambitious creations of the manufacture, these timepieces combined musical striking mechanisms with the brandÃ¢ÂÂs celebrated tourbillon architecture.
The present Opera Two represents one of the most sophisticated interpretations within the series. Produced in an exceedingly small number, each example required approximately 500 hours of meticulous hand assembly and finishing. At its heart lies a Westminster carillon minute repeater, an exceptionally complex mechanism that strikes the time on four gongs to reproduce the celebrated chimes of the Houses of Parliament in London. Within the movement, four hammers strike in sequence to recreate the distinctive Ã¢ÂÂBig BenÃ¢ÂÂ melody.
Further elevating the watchÃ¢ÂÂs visual appeal is its striking grey dial, decorated with a dramatic sunburst pattern radiating from the tourbillon aperture, enhancing the dynamic presence of the rotating cage.
The watch is accompanied by its impressive Girard-Perregaux wooden Ã¢ÂÂÃÂ©crin ÃÂ  rÃÂ©sonanceÃ¢ÂÂ presentation box, specially designed to amplify the sound of the repeater through a resonance soundboard. Engraved to the case back is the inscription Ã¢ÂÂUnique Set,Ã¢ÂÂ confirming the exceptional nature of the ensemble.
Preserved in unworn, like-new condition and offered complete with its box and accessories, the present Opera Two represents a remarkable expression of modern haute horlogerie.

Preserved in excellent condition, the present minute repeater represents the highest level of craftsmanship achieved by A. Lange & SÃÂ¶hne. Between 1845 and 1945, the firm produced approximately 369 minute repeating watches, with ÃÂ©bauches often supplied by movement makers such as LeCoultre & Co. in Le Sentier.Â The present example is fitted with a movement of the highest 1A quality, the pinnacle of LangeÃ¢ÂÂs production. In addition to exceptional finishing, it features diamond chatons, and a gold escapement; all executed to the highest standards.Â Notably, unlike the more commonly encountered Louis XV-style cases, this watch is housed in a refined and slim polished gold case, lending it a more understated and elegant appearance.Â Following the economic difficulties of the 1920s, the manufacture was compelled to introduce lower-grade Ã¢ÂÂDUFÃ¢ÂÂ minute repeaters, making high-grade 1A examples from this period exceptionally rare. The present watch therefore stands as a particularly scarce and important survivor of LangeÃ¢ÂÂs finest pre-war production.

Founded in 1845 by Ferdinand Adolph Lange in GlashÃÂ¼tte, A. Lange & SÃÂ¶hne quickly established itself as one of EuropeÃ¢ÂÂs foremost makers of precision timekeepers, renowned for its scientific instruments, marine chronometers, and highly accurate pocket watches. From its earliest years, the manufacture pursued chronometric excellence through rigorous construction standards and uncompromising hand craftsmanship, laying the foundations of Saxon watchmaking at its highest level.
Pocket chronometer no. 27885 is one of approximately 34 examples produced by the firm between 1883 and 1936, representing one of the rarest and most technically sophisticated categories within LangeÃ¢ÂÂs historical production. For a comprehensive list of these exceptional timepieces, including the present lot, see Martin Huber, Die Lange Liste, 2000, pp. 100Ã¢ÂÂ101, table 19. The watch is further illustrated in the same publication (p. 105, pl. 8), where its original sale on 27 November 1895 for 950 Marks to C. Schmutzer of Munich is recorded, underscoring its status as a costly and prestigious precision instrument at the time.
Although housed in the dimensions of a pocket watch, the present timepiece is constructed according to the principles of a fully fledged marine chronometer. In addition to its spring detent escapement, the movement is fitted with a fusee and chain transmission, ensuring a constant delivery of power from the mainspring and enhancing rate stability across the duration of the power reserve. The inclusion of a helical hairspring further advances timing precision by promoting more concentric balance oscillation. Taken together, these features elevate the watch to the highest echelon of chronometric performance and reflect A.Ã¢ÂÂ¯LangeÃ¢ÂÂ¯&Ã¢ÂÂ¯SÃÂ¶hneÃ¢ÂÂs ultimate pursuit of absolute accuracy.
The movement itself is of exceptional beauty, displaying LangeÃ¢ÂÂs signature three quarter plate construction, an exquisitely hand engraved balance cock, and a refined, highly legible architecture emblematic of the finest traditions of Saxon watchmaking. The use of the spring detent escapement, a technically demanding system in which impulse is delivered directly to the balance with minimal friction, firmly situates this watch among the elite precision timekeepers of its era, traditionally reserved for marine and observatory grade chronometers.
The rarity of such watches cannot be overstated. To the best of our knowledge, only around ten A. Introduced in 2007, the UR-201 stands as a foundational creation in UrwerkÃ¢ÂÂs early development, embodying the brandÃ¢ÂÂs radical rethinking of time display and mechanical interaction. Introduced in 1917 by Louis Cartier, the Tank by Cartier remains one of the most iconic wristwatch designs in horology. With its unusual mystery display, this 1970s Tortue by Cartier presents a striking fusion of modernist aesthetics and Art Deco innovation. First launched in the mid 1980s, the Ã¢ÂÂTrilogy of TimeÃ¢ÂÂ was conceived as a tribute to three of the most influential figures in astronomy: Galileo Galilei, Nicolaus Copernicus, and Johannes Kepler.

These Peruvian Air Force-issued watches can be identified by several distinctive details. Throughout the 1970s Rolex supplied watches to the British Military for use by the Special Forces, namely the Rolex Submariner. The Rolex Explorer reference 6350 holds a pivotal place in the history of Rolex as the first model to bear the Explorer designation on its dial. Introduced in 1953, the same year Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the summit of Mount Everest, it followed earlier references 6150 and 6098, which were Precision models.
The reference 6350 was predominantly fitted with a honeycomb dial, as seen on the present example, featuring the correct chapter ring and OCC designation for Officially Certified Chronometer at 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock. Its robust case was engineered to withstand extreme conditions, protecting the calibre A296 movement within.
More than a technical achievement, the 6350 represents the genesis of RolexÃ¢ÂÂs professional watch lineage, paving the way for models such as the Submariner, GMT-Master, and Daytona.
The present example has aged beautifully, with its gilt signature echoed by the warm patina of the indexes, while the honeycomb dial plays elegantly with the light, adding depth and character to this rare and historically important timepiece.

The Explorer 1655 is often referred to by the nickname 'Freccione' (Italian for 'arrow') thanks to its very prominent arrow-tipped orange 24-hour hand. By pointing to the fixed 24-hour marked bezel, the orange 24-hour hand serves as a prominent day or night indicator; vital for those who spend extended periods exploring in hazardous conditions and might otherwise become disorientated.This watch is from the first series, which is also the most collectible one. Watches belonging to this original production have serial numbers between 2.5 and 3.5million. Its most important difference is the straight seconds hand that was only used during that production period.This lot has aged beautifully with indexes gaining a warm patina, perfectly complementing the bright orange hand.

Rolex and COMEX Compagnie Maritime d'Expertises shared a common commitment to technical excellence and engineering innovation. While Rolex brought its expertise in precision watchmaking, COMEX operated at the forefront of deep sea exploration for the oil industry. Together, they pushed the boundaries of what was possible, developing specialised Submariners for professional divers, some equipped with helium escape valves in the mid to late 1960s to prevent damage caused by helium accumulation during saturation diving.
The present watch is a reference 5513, one of the purest expressions of the Submariner line. Produced from 1962 to 1989, the 5513 is characterised by its no date dial, symmetrical layout, and robust construction, making it a natural choice for professional use and a frequent base for COMEX issued timepieces.
The present example, with a 2.8 million case number dating to circa 1970, displays the quintessential two lines of text indicating its 660 ft depth rating and the model designation Ã¢ÂÂSubmariner,Ã¢ÂÂ with the COMEX logo prominently positioned beneath the centre. The case is fitted with a helium escape valve on the left hand side, while the COMEX engraving and number Ã¢ÂÂ24Ã¢ÂÂ remain visible on the case back. Inside, the case back is stamped III.70 and bears the last three digits of the serial, Ã¢ÂÂ552,Ã¢ÂÂ further supporting the watchÃ¢ÂÂs authenticity and coherence.

Fresh to the market from a Scandinavian deepÃ¢ÂÂsea diver, the present Rolex SeaÃ¢ÂÂDweller Ref. 16660 is distinguished by an exceptional and fully professional history. Originally issued directly by COMEX Compagnie Maritime dÃ¢ÂÂExpertises, the legendary French deepÃ¢ÂÂsea engineering enterprise, the watch was first assigned to a French COMEX diver named Godart. Over the course of nine years, he carried it on demanding missions across the globe, relying on the watch through pressurized chambers, saturation dives, and extended decompression periods.
In 1991, during a 450Ã¢ÂÂmeter saturation dive in the North Sea, to the consignorÃ¢ÂÂs knowledge the deepest dive ever performed with this specific watch, Mr Godart met the Scandinavian diver Mr. Johansson who would become its next custodian. After 33 days working together in extreme conditions, the two surfaced as friends, and Mr Johansson acquired the watch directly from Mr Godart. Johansson then continued to use it throughout his own deepÃ¢ÂÂsea diving career until 2005, giving this example an uninterrupted life as a true professional tool worn in service by two saturation divers over more than two decades.
The reference 16660, known among collectors as the Ã¢ÂÂTriple Six,Ã¢ÂÂ represents a pivotal transitional moment in the evolution of the SeaÃ¢ÂÂDweller. Featuring a newly strengthened case, sapphire crystal, and an enlarged helium escape valve, the modelÃ¢ÂÂs technical advancements increased its depth rating to an impressive 1220 meters (4000 feet). Inside the case, Rolex introduced the Caliber 3035, replacing the earlier 1575 movement used in the preceding reference 1665 and marking a significant mechanical upgrade.
Long believed to have been produced with matte dials only for the first 50 examples, collectorÃ¢ÂÂled research has since shown that the entire original COMEX batch, numbered 3001 to 3099, was in fact delivered with matte dials, with some later replaced by Rolex with glossy service dials during routine maintenance. The present watch is one of these rare early Ref 16660 COMEXÃ¢ÂÂissued pieces that still retains its original matte dial. Repeating serial number inside the case back, and original punched guarantee paper, further underscoring its authenticity and desirability among specialists and collectors.
Issued exclusively to COMEX personnel and never offered to the public, these SeaÃ¢ÂÂDwellers are among the most coveted of all Rolex tool watches. Their COMEXÃ¢ÂÂsigned dials, internal case back identification numbers, and proven utilitarian provenance distinguish them as the purest expression of the Rolex COMEX partnership, one of the most celebrated collaborations in the history of professional diving instrumentation.
Uniting genuine COMEX issue and a deeply compelling twoÃ¢ÂÂdiver history culminating in a 450Ã¢ÂÂmeter North Sea saturation mission, this Ref. 16660 No 3067 stands as an extraordinary example of a SeaÃ¢ÂÂDweller whose life was not simply documented, but truly lived at depth.

The origin of the IWC Portugieser dates back to the 1930's when two Portuguese businessmen, Rodrigues and Teixeira, visited the IWCÂ factory proposing the development of a large stainless steel wristwatch housing a movement that could match the precision of a marine chronometer, with perfect readability and the highest possible precision. This quest led to the introduction of the legendary reference 325 in 1939.Â The proportions of the pieces were extraordinary at the time. A 42mm case diameter was substantially larger than an normal timepiece of an average diameter just above 30mm. To power these watches, IWC first used their calibre 74, which was originally a pocket watch movement. According to the Manufacture, only 304 examples were powered by this calibre.Â This tool watch has now become an horological icon of the first part of the 20th century as well as an inspiration for generations of watch designers.
While the vast majority of these rare watches show heavy signs of age, especially to their dials, this present lot has its glossy dial preserved in most outstanding condition. Furthermore, the gilt signature and indexes are equally well preserved and contrast beautifully over the dial plate, creating a striking effect. The case is similarly preserved, further enhancing its desirability. This exceptional condition can be explained by the fact that this watch was preserved in its original presentation case, also accompanying the lot, for many decades and just recently rediscovered.

Designed as a tool watch for those who push the limits of exploration, the Explorer II was developed as a robust and highly legible evolution of the original threeÃ¢ÂÂhand Oyster Perpetual Explorer. Built to withstand high humidity, intense heat, and freezing temperatures, it was specifically intended for use in environments such as deep cave systems and highÃ¢ÂÂaltitude peaks. Rolex targeted speleologists and underground explorers who spent long periods without natural light and would benefit from the clear 24Ã¢ÂÂhour indication to tell day from night.
Launched in 1971, reference 1655 features a fixed steel bezel engraved with a 24Ã¢ÂÂhour scale and a distinctive large orange hand Ã¢ÂÂ the celebrated Freccione Ã¢ÂÂ allowing the wearer to distinguish day from night at a glance.
The model is closely associated with extreme explorations and mountaineering, personified by the most influential highÃ¢ÂÂaltitude climber of all time, Reinhold Messner. Field use under realÃ¢ÂÂworld conditions played a crucial role in RolexÃ¢ÂÂs ongoing technical refinement of its watches. Messner received such watches for use during his climbs, and was photographed wearing an Explorer II on numerous expeditions.Â 
The significance of the present reference 1655 extends far beyond its technical attributes. It was gifted by Reinhold Messner to his long-time expedition logistician, Prithivi Raj Chettri, known as Ã¢ÂÂBobby.Ã¢ÂÂ Bobby devoted his life to the meticulous planning and coordination of Himalayan treks and more than 60 major expeditions, including the 1978 Austrian Everest Expedition led by Wolfgang Nairz Ã¢ÂÂ during which Messner and Peter Habelar achieved the first ascent of Mount Everest without supplemental oxygen.In pursuits shaped by nature Ã¢ÂÂ where conditions dictate outcome and fate is never entirely oneÃ¢ÂÂs own Ã¢ÂÂ trust and bond is everything. Over years of shared objectives, risks, and achievements, Messner and Bobby developed a friendship that transcended their profession. Messner spent countless evenings with Bobby and his family, becoming closely woven into their lives. To commemorate their bond, Messner gifted Bobby one of his personal watches: the present Rolex Explorer II, dating from 1979.Â 
Consigned by the family of the original owner, the watch is accompanied by a letter from Messner to BobbyÃ¢ÂÂs son, photographs as well as MessnerÃ¢ÂÂs own ice axe Ã¢ÂÂ elements that add exceptional historical and collector interest. The accompanying guarantee, stamped by RolexÃ¢ÂÂs German headquarters in Cologne, Germany, and signed by Herr KÃÂ¶nig confirms that the watch was not commercially retailed but issued directly to Messner, further reinforcing its exceptional provenance.Â Produced until the midÃ¢ÂÂ1980s, reference 1655 was issued with five distinct dial variations. The present watch displays the Mk 4 dial with serifÃ¢ÂÂstyle Ã¢ÂÂT SWISS 
Adding to its desirability, this early example is accompanied by its full set of original accessories, together with exceptional Reinhold Messner memorabilia, including his ice axe, signed photographs, and personal correspondence between Messner and the consignor, as well as a letter attesting to the watchÃ¢ÂÂs provenance, further enhancing its historical importance and uniqueness.
A watch shaped by the most demanding environments and enriched by a deeply personal story, the present Rolex Explorer II reference 1655 rises far beyond its function. Opportunities to acquire such a complete and historically significant example remain exceedingly rare, offering collectors the chance to secure not only an icon of Rolex, but a true piece of mountaineering history.

During the 1920s and 1930s, the rise of leisure and sporting pursuits encouraged watchmakers to develop innovative case designs offering greater protection. Among these, Cartier introduced its elegant shutter form wristwatch, derived from the Sac ÃÂ  Guillotine BÃÂ©bÃÂ© purse watch, creating a distinctive and highly refined solution to the Ã¢ÂÂprotectedÃ¢ÂÂ watch concept alongside contemporaries such as the Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso. Ordered by Cartier London, it is believed that only around 50 ÃÂclipse Guillotine wristwatches were produced for the English market in the 1930s. While closely related to earlier purse watch designs, the case was carefully reworked with pronounced downturned lugs and smooth, polished surfaces to enhance comfort on the wrist. The signature sliding shutters, based on systems developed and patented by Edmond Jaeger from 1909 onwards and refined in 1928, offer both protection and a captivating display, exemplifying a perfect balance between form and function. The cases were manufactured by Georges Larmanger, a specialist in guillotine purse watch production. Notably, these wristwatch models feature plain polished case sides and backs, unlike the purse watch versions, whose decoration extended across the entire case, a refinement that further improved wearability.
A striking example of avant garde design, the present watch is further distinguished by a hand engraved inscription to the case back reading Ã¢ÂÂGaspard June 7th 1931,Ã¢ÂÂ adding a layer of personal history to an already rare and technically inventive timepiece.

A rare and early decorative cushion-form model, the caseÃ¢ÂÂs bezel is filled with black enamel which is interspersed with a repeated gold Ã¢ÂÂdotÃ¢ÂÂ motif. This design can be found on a small number of other models from the period, including CarrÃÂ©, Tank and Tonneau models. The watch is also notable for its early Edmond Jaeger design deployant clasp that has a rectangular clasp closure.

The Reverso case was developed by the designer RenÃÂ©-Alfred Chauvot, who filed his patent in France under no. 712.868 on 4 March 1931. The patent application was described as being for: Ã¢ÂÂ[Une] Montre susceptible de coulisser dans son support et pouvant se retourner complÃÂ¨tement sur elle-mÃÂªmeÃ¢ÂÂ, that is, a watch that could slide within a holder and turn completely upon itself. The French patent was granted on 14 October 1931, and the rights were purchased, before publication, by the Swiss businessman CÃÂ©sar de Trey. In November the same year, de Trey formed a marketing company with Jacques-David LeCoultre called SpÃÂ©cialitÃÂ©s HorlogÃÂ¨res in order to market the Reverso. 
During the early years of the ReversoÃ¢ÂÂs production, a small number of Reverso cases were sold to other companies, including Cartier, Patek Philippe and Vacheron Constantin. However, in 1934, SpÃÂ©cialitÃÂ©s HorlogÃÂ¨res was renamed the SociÃÂ©tÃÂ© de Vente des Produits Jaeger-LeCoultre, and it was this firm that acquired the Reverso patent. The ReversoÃ¢ÂÂs primary aim was to protect the glass of the watch, and from the outset the model was aimed at the sportsman. It is said that CÃÂ©sar de Trey had originally approached Chauvot to design a watch that could withstand the rough and tumble of a game of polo Ã¢ÂÂ de Trey had apparently seen a gap in the market when challenged to produce a shock-proof watch by a polo player whose watch glass had just been broken during a match. 
With its elegant, clean lines and rectangular shape, the watchÃ¢ÂÂs design was perfectly suited to the Art Deco period. Reversing to a plain back, the watch also offered the tempting possibility for the buyer to personalise their watch with their own initials, their family crest or a unique decorative motif. Early advertisements for the model already showed examples with monochrome, enamel-decorated initials and monograms. However, the reversing inner case also allowed for the introduction of a secondary dial on its back. 
Although Jaeger LeCoultre did not officially introduce a series-produced dual-dial Reverso until the 1990s, Cartier had already taken advantage of the design by the 1970s, producing versions with two dials, such as the example shown here Ã¢ÂÂ one on the front and one on the back of the revolving inner case Ã¢ÂÂ each powered by its own movement and set from an individual winding crown. This ingenious dual-time watch features dials in contrasting colours, making it easy to distinguish between the two. The winding crowns are subtly recessed into the case so that only the crown corresponding to the visible dial is exposed at any given time. Although thicker than CartierÃ¢ÂÂs slimmer reversible wristwatch with a single dial, the addition of a second movement and dial increases the thickness by little more than 2.5mm.

The oversized Ã¢ÂÂTank HichamÃ¢ÂÂ XL forms part of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs elusive SteppedÃ¢ÂÂCase family of the midÃ¢ÂÂ1970s, one of the most intriguing and least documented chapters of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs preÃ¢ÂÂmust de Cartier era. Produced in small boutiqueÃ¢ÂÂspecific batches for Paris, London and New York, these watches are recognised for their sharply tiered bezel, painted Roman numerals and bold reinterpretation of the classic Tank aesthetic during a period when CartierÃ¢ÂÂs major boutiques still operated independently.
With limited examples made for both Paris, London, and New York, well preserved survivors are extremely rare, due to dial ageing, heavy wear, and the fragile goldÃ¢ÂÂplated brass cases.
Crucially, the SteppedÃ¢ÂÂCase designs anticipated CartierÃ¢ÂÂs strategic shift toward accessible luxury. They stand as a preÃ¢ÂÂcollection precursorÂ to the philosophy that would later define the Must de Cartier line, culminating in the launch of the Tank Must in 1977, a model that reintroduced the Tank to a wider audience with colourful dials, plated cases, and a modern reinterpretation of Louis CartierÃ¢ÂÂs 1917 design.
Bold, sculptural and historically significant, the Tank Hicham XL remains one of the most distinctive gold plated Tank variants of the 1970s and an important link between CartierÃ¢ÂÂs boutique creativity and the Cartier collection we know today.

In 1979, the Paris, London, and New York branches of Cartier were unified under a single entity, Cartier World. To commemorate this milestone, the maison released a series of limited edition wristwatches in platinum, including models such as the Baignoire, Ellipse, Santos, Tank LC, Tortue, and VendÃÂ´me. These pieces were distinguished by specially designed dials featuring burgundy Roman numerals and ruby cabochon set crowns, a design language later revisited for subsequent commemorative editions.
The present Santos exemplifies this rare series in an exceptionally refined execution. An ultra slim interpretation of the iconic model, it is powered by the FrÃÂ©dÃÂ©ric Piguet calibre 21, measuring just 1.75 mm in height. Once cased, the watch achieves an overall thickness of only 4.5 mm, underscoring CartierÃ¢ÂÂs mastery of elegant, slim proportions.

The Cartier Tank CintrÃÂ©e, first introduced in 1921, is one of the most elegant and enduring watch designs of the 20th century. Defined by its elongated, slim rectangular case that gracefully curves to follow the natural contour of the wrist, the CintrÃÂ©e was a triumph of both ergonomics and aesthetics. Unlike many rectangular watches, which rely on hinges or friction fittings, the CintrÃÂ©eÃ¢ÂÂs case back is securely pressed into the upper case and held by small screws, creating a seamless integration that ensures a sleek and refined profile. Over the decades, the model has remained a rare and highly sought-after timepiece, typically available only by special order. 
One of the notable distinctions of Cartier London was its experimentation with numeral colouration. The use of blue numerals is extremely unusual in vintage Cartier watches, yet Cartier London offered or customised dials with the option of red or blue numerals instead of black as highlighted in the present example and is hallmarked for the same year cycle as this watchÃ¢ÂÂs case (1969Ã¢ÂÂ70).

Introduced in 1951, the J.J.C. Tank by Cartier was developed by Jean-Jacques Cartier as a distinct interpretation of the original Louis Cartier model. Defined by its softly rounded brancards, it reflects the more expressive and unconventional design language of the London workshop.
The present example, dating from 1971Ã¢ÂÂ72, is a refined expression of this lineage. Cased in 18k yellow gold and bearing London hallmarks, it retains the classic proportions of the Tank, complemented by a beaded crown set with a blue sapphire cabochon.
It is, however, through the dial that the London identity is most clearly expressed. The hand painted enamel dial omits the traditional chemin de fer minute track, a signature feature of Cartier London pieces, while the elongated Roman numerals create a more open and graphic composition. Paired with blued steel ÃÂ©pÃÂ©e hands, the result is a strikingly pure and characterful interpretation of one of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs most iconic designs.

The reference 5159 by Patek Philippe was introduced in 2007, replacing the earlier reference 5059. It distinguished itself through a slightly enlarged, classically styled case, increased by 2 mm, and the addition of a finely hand engraved dial.
A perpetual calendar, the model displays the day, date, month, leap year, and moon phases, with the retrograde date indication providing a dynamic and highly legible focal point. It is powered by the self-winding calibre 324 S QR, visible beneath the officer style hinged case back, a feature that enhances both practicality and charm. 
The combination of these elements gives the reference 5159 a timeless and distinctive character, drawing on some of Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs most iconic design codes while showcasing the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs dedication to traditional craftsmanship.

The Patek Philippe Annual Calendar reference 5205R-001 stands as an exquisite example of Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs modern interpretation of the annual calendar complication.Introduced as part of the evolution of the reference 5205 line, first unveiled in 2010, the present rose gold variant was launched in 2013, following the initial white gold executions. It reflects the brandÃ¢ÂÂs continued refinement of one of its most practical complications, requiring adjustment only once per year.Housed in an innovative 40 mm case, the watch embodies the essence of a contemporary dress timepiece. The design is further elevated by its distinctive openworked lugs, gracefully downturned to follow the natural contours of the wrist.The dial is particularly well balanced, with day, date, and month displayed through three apertures at 12 oÃ¢ÂÂclock, complemented by a moon phase and 24 hour indication at 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock, ensuring both clarity and visual harmony.Preserved in very good overall condition, the present example retains well-defined case proportions, with crisp hallmarks beneath the lugs and only light signs of wear, enhancing its overall appeal.

This exceptionally rare timepiece embodies both charisma and refined elegance. Very few examples of early rectangular white gold watches by Patek Philippe are known, and they seldom appear on the market.
Historically, such designs mark a pivotal moment in the evolution of the wristwatch, moving away from their pocket watch origins to embrace new forms and a more independent identity. Aesthetically, the emphasis shifts from pure function to the pursuit of beauty as an object in its own right.

At the time, white gold examples were produced in extremely limited numbers, as the majority of pieces were cased in yellow gold, further enhancing the rarity of the present watch.
Uniting historical importance, aesthetic refinement, and scarcity, this timepiece represents a compelling opportunity for the discerning collector.

The reference 2441 by Patek Philippe was introduced in 1948 and remained in production until the late 1950s. Nicknamed the Ã¢ÂÂEiffel Tower,Ã¢ÂÂ it owes its name to the distinctive flared case design, inspired by the architectural base lines of the Eiffel Tower. The case was manufactured by Markowski, identifiable by the key hallmark with the number 8 inside the caseback.
Powering the watch is the celebrated calibre 9'''90, an emblematic tonneau-shaped movement that perfectly complements the curvature of the case, reflecting Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs attention to both form and function.
Beyond its technical merit, the reference 2441 stands out for its bold departure from traditional round case designs of the period, embodying a more expressive and architectural approach to wristwatch design. According to scholarship, only around 110 examples were cased in yellow gold, underscoring the rarity of the present model.
A striking and highly recognisable creation, the reference 2441 remains one of the most charismatic and collectible vintage Patek Philippe designs.

Launched in 1950, the reference 2481 represents a significant evolution of the Calatrava, offering a larger 37 mm diameter case. It was remarkably oversized for its time compared to the more traditional 32 mm diameter examples. Often referred to as the Ã¢ÂÂKing Size,Ã¢ÂÂ the case was made by Le Locle Master Casemaker Bernard Dubois, identified by the number 171 in the hammer head, and introduced new proportions that would remain highly appealing to modern collectors.
The present reference 2481J exemplifies this balance, combining timeless elegance with a forward-thinking case size, making it a particularly desirable iteration within the Calatrava lineage. 
Preserved in overall very appealing condition, the watch was recently serviced by Patek Philippe and retains its service case back sticker.

Produced from 1958 to the 1970s, the reference 3417 by Patek Philippe was the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs first serially produced anti-magnetic wristwatch, reflecting the growing need for precision in environments exposed to strong magnetic fields. Powered by the calibre 12Ã¢ÂÂ AM-400, later upgraded to the 27 AM-400, the movement is protected by a soft iron inner case and fitted with a gold lever to ensure accuracy, while also offering water-resistant and dust-proof properties. Alongside its integrated bracelet counterpart, the reference 3418, it remains one of the only vintage Patek Philippe wristwatches produced exclusively in stainless steel prior to the Nautilus.
Beyond its technical innovation, the reference 3417 is admired for its restrained yet distinctive design, combining clean Bauhaus-inspired elements with the characteristic Ã¢ÂÂAmagneticÃ¢ÂÂ script on the dial. Dating from the mid-1960s, the present example features a Series 2 dial, identifiable by its smaller subsidiary seconds, indexes positioned closer to the dialÃ¢ÂÂs edge, and the specific spacing of the Ã¢ÂÂIÃ¢ÂÂ in the Ã¢ÂÂPATEK PHILIPPEÃ¢ÂÂ signature.
Preserved in attractive condition and accompanied by its Extract from the Archives, this watch represents a rare opportunity to acquire one of the brandÃ¢ÂÂs earliest and most historically important tool wristwatches.

Patek Philippe marked its 175th anniversary with a series of exclusive commemorative timepieces, including the highly sought-after reference 5975 Multi-Scale Chronograph. Produced in a strictly limited run of just 400 examples in pink gold, this exceptional wristwatch showcases three logarithmic scales: a tachymeter for measuring speed, a telemeter for calculating distance, and a pulsometer for tracking heart rate. 
Beyond its functional appeal, the multi-scale chronograph design carries strong historical resonance, having been especially popular during the era of the World War II. In this sense, reference 5975 stands as both a technical instrument and a tribute to horological heritage, reinterpreted for the modern collector.
At the heart of the watch lies the CH 28-520 self-winding movement, developed specifically for this model. This sophisticated calibre features a traditional column wheel to control the chronograph functions, along with an advanced disk clutch system that minimizes friction and allows the central chronograph hand to run continuously as a seconds display. 
Operating at 21,600 vibrations per hour and offering a power reserve of at least 50 hours, the movement reflects the pinnacle of precision engineering.

Founded in 1878 by Gerhard Diedrich Wilhelm Wempe, Wempe has grown from a German workshop into an international presence. Since 1972, under the direction of Herbert Wempe, the firm has held an official license to retail timepieces from Patek Philippe in Hamburg.
Introduced in 2003, the reference 5125 was created to celebrate WempeÃ¢ÂÂs 125th anniversary and its longstanding relationship with Patek Philippe. The model was produced in a limited edition of 125 pieces in each gold colour and 100 examples in platinum.
This annual calendar is distinguished by the retailerÃ¢ÂÂs name proudly displayed on the moon phase subsidiary dial, further enhanced by its striking dark dial, which adds depth and a contemporary elegance to the display.
The present example is offered with all its original accessories, representing a rare and highly attractive commemorative edition.

The Patek Philippe reference 5101 is a highly complicated timepiece that embodies the discreetness and understatement so characteristic of Patek Philippe. Affectionately known as the Ã¢ÂÂMarathon RunnerÃ¢ÂÂ for its exceptional 10-day power reserve, it was introduced in 2003, with approximately 500 examples produced in platinum. Its striking triple stepped case flanks recall the firmÃ¢ÂÂs celebrated Art Deco designs of the 1920s and 1930s, while the curved case and convex sapphire crystal ensure exceptional comfort on the wrist.

The second complication, a one minute tourbillon composed of 72 components and weighing just 0.3 grams, is deliberately hidden on the dial side in keeping with Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs philosophy of preserving precision by shielding it from light and shocks. It is instead revealed through the sapphire case back, where the refined finishing of the movement can be fully appreciated.
A rare blend of technical mastery, architectural design, and understated elegance, the reference 5101 stands as one of the most distinctive modern creations from Patek Philippe.

The Patek Philippe reference 5013R was introduced in 1992 as Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs first automatic wristwatch combining a perpetual calendar with a retrograde date and a minute repeater. It remained in production until 2010.
The 5013R represents one of the most desirable iterations of the reference, pairing exceptional rarity with the superior acoustic qualities of rose gold, widely regarded as an ideal metal for minute repeater resonance. At its heart lies the calibre R 27 PS QR, the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs first automatic minute repeater. Its 22k gold micro-rotor preserves a slim profile while powering a mechanism composed of 515 finely crafted components. As with all Patek Philippe minute repeaters, each example is individually hand tuned, ensuring a unique and exceptional acoustic signature.
A remarkable synthesis of technical mastery and refined aesthetics, the reference stands as a discreet yet powerful expression of Patek PhilippeÃ¢ÂÂs grand complication expertise, offering a rare opportunity to acquire a truly exceptional timepiece.

A genius in fine watchmaking, F. P. Journe is known for mind-blowing inventions whilst constantly seeking perfection in complicated watches. His hard work throughout the years was well acknowledged by the horological community for being the first to win the celebrated Aiguille dÃ¢ÂÂOr prize three times, and the current Centigraphe was the collection that made his crown for the 3rdÂ time.

In 1971, Rolex gave its chronograph range a major update, introducing a series of enhancements that modernised the design and made the watch far more suited to the demands of sport and speed. Introduced in 1963, the reference 6239 marked the beginning of the Rolex Cosmograph Daytona and the emergence of one of the most celebrated chronographs ever produced by Rolex. It was the first to bear the Cosmograph designation and introduced key design evolutions, notably the tachymeter scale relocated from the dial to the bezel, allowing for a clearer and more dynamic dial layout. The model also debuted contrasting subsidiary dials, enhancing legibility while giving rise to a highly distinctive aesthetic.
The present example is particularly notable for its Paul Newman dial, famously associated with Paul Newman following his appearance wearing the watch during the promotion of the 1969 film Winning. Its three colour black dial, with white outer track and red accents echoed in the Daytona signature, is beautifully preserved and offers a striking visual presence.
Fitted with a bezel graduated to 300 units, a calibre 722-1, and a 7835 riveted bracelet, the watch reflects one of the final evolutions of the reference before its replacement at the end of the decade. Considered among the greatest in F1 history, Michael Schumacher gave this watch to Nigel Stepney after the 2000 Spanish Grand Prix incident.
The story behind the present watch begins with Michael Schumacher at the centre of one of the most unforgettable moments of the 2000 Formula One season. During the Spanish Grand Prix at the Circuit de Catalunya, amid the roar of engines and the tension of an early championship battle, FerrariÃ¢ÂÂs race unfolded with devastating speed, until a single pitÃ¢ÂÂstop changed everything. A refuelling malfunction ignited a sudden burst of flames around the Ferrari pit crew, and in the chaos that followed, the accelerating car struck senior team member Nigel Stepney, running over his leg in full view of the worldÃ¢ÂÂs cameras. The incident, remains one of the most dramatic and replayed pitÃ¢ÂÂlane accidents of the era.
Nigel Stepney (1958Ã¢ÂÂ2014) was not an ordinary member of the team. A respected and influential Formula One mechanic who had contributed to multiple championship campaigns with Lotus, Benetton, and ultimately Ferrari, Stepney was part of the technical backbone that powered the teamÃ¢ÂÂs renaissance in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Calm under pressure, technically gifted, and deeply respected in the paddock, he was central to FerrariÃ¢ÂÂs operations during its most dominant period. His injury during that split second in Spain rocked the organisation and left a profound impact on those involved.
In the days following the incident, an unusually personal gesture unfolded within the Ferrari team. Michael Schumacher presented Nigel Stepney with his own Rolex Daytona Ref. 16518, an exceptional piece in remarkable condition and fitted with a rare MotherÃ¢ÂÂofÃ¢ÂÂPearl dial, further personalized by SchumacherÃ¢ÂÂs name engraved on the case back. He placed the watch inside a lacquered wooden Rolex box and inscribed the lid in sweeping metallic gold ink with a dedication: Ã¢ÂÂTo Nigel 2000!Ã¢ÂÂ accompanied by his signature. Offered directly as an apology and a gesture of goodwill after the accident, this gift stands as a rare and uniquely personal act from the legendary driver to a trusted team member.
More than a watch, it embodies a dramatic moment in racing history and the gesture that emerged from it.

A particularly bold and broad bezel accentuates the distinctive hexagonal form of this watch, dating to 1946. Defined by its six sided geometry, the case presents a striking and highly architectural profile, with the strong lines of the bezel echoed throughout the hexagonal chapter ring and minute track.
While Cartier has explored hexagonal shapes in other models, these are typically rendered with slimmer bezels or more stepped constructions. In contrast, the present example stands out for its seamless and balanced proportions, where the bold bezel reinforces the purity of the form.
A compelling expression of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs post war creativity, this watch highlights the maisonÃ¢ÂÂs ability to translate geometric design into an elegant and wearable timepiece.

The ÃÂtrier (stirrup) model, also referred to as the Calandre, was introduced by Cartier in 1921 and took advantage of the growing interest in the fashionable sport of horse racing.
In the 1920s, horse racing was highly popular in Europe, particularly in the UK and France, where prestigious events like the Epsom Derby and Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe attracted large crowds. The sport benefitted from the economic prosperity and growing leisure culture of the Ã¢ÂÂRoaring TwentiesÃ¢ÂÂ. It was associated with social status and became a fashionable activity, drawing both elite and everyday spectators. Betting played a major role in its appeal, with wagering systems enhancing the excitement.
In the U.S., races like the Kentucky Derby and the Triple Crown series also gained prominence, with legendary horses such as Man o' War bringing international attention to American racing.
Hallmarked for 1976-77, this is one of the last wristwatches to be made in the Wright and Davies workshops. Watches made at Cartier in London were handmade in very small numbers and as the ÃÂtrier does not appear to have been a model in general production at the time, this watch may well have been a special order. Edmond JaegerÃ¢ÂÂs patent No. 157094, filed on 16 April 1931, describes an innovative watch design featuring a sliding cover mechanism. The mechanism is seamlessly integrated into the watch case, preserving the timepieceÃ¢ÂÂs elegant appearance. CartierÃ¢ÂÂs adoption of this case design in its Baguette model underscores the firmÃ¢ÂÂs commitment to innovative watchmaking. 
The design features a unique mechanism where the central panel of the case slides to reveal the dial. This ingenious feature adds both functionality and a sense of intrigue to the timepiece while protecting the dial when not in use. The placement of the winding crown to the case back ensures that the modelÃ¢ÂÂs clean lines remain uninterrupted. 
The sliding cover not only adds elegance but also serves a practical purpose, making the watch particularly suited to active lifestyles. Much like the Cartier Basculante or Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso, it offers a clever solution for dial protection and is ideal for sporting activities.

One of the most iconic designs from CartierÃ¢ÂÂs vintage production, the ParallÃÂ©logramme, transforms the traditional rectangular Tank form case by twisting it to an oblique angle. The dial mirrors this off-set design, forming a lozenge shape with the 12 and 6 oÃ¢ÂÂclock markers positioned at the top right and lower left corners of the case, respectively. This unconventional arrangement allowed the time to be quickly and easily read at an angle Ã¢ÂÂ for instance, when the wrist was outstretched in front of the wearer, such as resting on a table or on the steering wheel of a car. A similar angled layout was a popular feature of early driverÃ¢ÂÂs watches.
Originally introduced in 1936, the ParallÃÂ©logramme represents a modernist expression of the late Art Deco period. Its bold and innovative design can be seen as one of the final flourishes of this artistic movement before the onset of the Second World War, which ushered in a more austere and functional era in watchmaking, prioritizing simplicity and practicality over experimentation. However, it is important to remember that the introduction of the ParallÃÂ©logramme occurred during the early development of the wristwatch genre, a time when Swiss wristwatch exports had only recently surpassed those of pocket watches. Without long-standing design precedents for wristwatches, this innovative approach reflected the experimental spirit of the era.
Although now commonly referred to as the Tank AsymÃÂ©trique, this model was not originally part of the Tank line and was officially named the ParallÃÂ©logramme. An extract from the Cartier Archives dated 24 September 1936 describes a Ã¢ÂÂBracelet Montre or ParallÃÂ©logram, ModÃÂ¨le 385Ã¢ÂÂ with a leather strap and gold pin buckle. This aforementioned watch, numbered 74951 / 50668, was sold on 17 December 1936 for Fr. 2,200 (with the archives noting the production cost as Fr. 1,190). The AsymÃÂ©trique was originally produced in two distinct styles: the ParallÃÂ©logramme, matching the watch illustrated here, and the Losange ÃÂ  Brides, which featured an additional central lug that created a hinge-like formation and into which the strap was integrated.
This modelÃ¢ÂÂs striking design has inspired several re-releases over the decades. In her book The Cartiers, Francesca Cartier-Brickell notes that this design was one of her grandfatherÃ¢ÂÂs, Jean-Jacques CartierÃ¢ÂÂs, favourites and the London workshops produced a limited number of ParallÃÂ©logramme watches. Later, new limited editions of the design, now popularly known as the Tank AsymÃÂ©trique, were introduced in 1996, 1999, 2009, and most recently in 2020 as part of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs exclusive Collection PrivÃÂ©.

Tanis, an ancient city in the Nile River delta, was a site of major archaeological discovery, and in the 1930s French excavations there uncovered gold masks and jewellery in gold and silver. The Cartier Baignoire S is a striking expression of CartierÃ¢ÂÂs ability to transform a classic design into a sculptural work of haute joaillerie.Rooted in the Baignoire lineage introduced in 1906, the present interpretation reimagines the form through an elongated Ã¢ÂÂSÃ¢ÂÂ-shaped case in 18k pink gold, entirely set with brilliant-cut diamonds that follow its complex curves, creating a dynamic play of light. This impressive cocktail watch elevates CartierÃ¢ÂÂs iconic Tortue form to new heights of refinement through its intricate diamond embellishments. Perfectly aligned with the emerging Art Deco aesthetic, the result is a composition of remarkable delicacy, structure, and enduring elegance.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Concept GMT Tourbillon, reference 26560IO.OO.D002CA.01, exemplifies the manufactureÃ¢ÂÂs forward-looking approach to contemporary watchmaking. The Urwerk UR-105 TA is presented here as a unique example, underscoring UrwerkÃ¢ÂÂs reputation for experimental, one off creations. Introduced in 2015, the Legacy Machine Perpetual by MB&F reimagined the perpetual calendar from first principles.
